decks.title: Constructions — Part 1: Tangents from an external point
goals: State that a tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact
Construct the two tangents from an external point to a circle, with steps of construction
Calculate the length of a tangent and the angle between two tangents, and check against measurement
Solve problems on concentric circles and on tangents inclined at a given angle

slides.heading: Tangents from a point: construction
slides.body_md: A **tangent** touches a circle at exactly one point. From a point **outside** a circle you can draw **two** tangents, and with ruler and compasses you can construct them exactly.

visual.alt: A circle with centre O and radius 3 centimetres. P is a point outside the circle with OP equal to 5 centimetres. Two tangents PA and PB touch the circle at A and B; each is 4 centimetres long and carries one tick. The radii OA and OB are dashed and meet the tangents at right angles.
visual.caption: Two tangents from $P$ to a circle of radius $3$ cm: $PA = PB = 4$ cm. Lengths in cm.

slides.narration: Welcome to constructions. Here a circle with centre O has a point P outside it. Two straight lines from P just touch the circle, at A and at B. These are the tangents. They are equal in length, here four centimetres each, and each is at a right angle to the radius at its point of contact. In this part we construct them and measure them.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Use the **right angle** between a tangent and a radius
Follow and write the **steps of construction** of the tangents
Find the **length** of a tangent and the **angle** between two tangents
Handle **concentric circles** and tangents at a given angle
slides.narration: These are your goals for part one. You will use the right angle between a tangent and a radius. You will follow and write the steps of the construction. You will find the length of a tangent and the angle between two tangents, and you will solve problems on concentric circles.

slides.heading: A tangent and the radius to its point of contact
slides.body_md: A tangent meets the circle in **one point** $T$, the **point of contact**. The radius $OT$ is **perpendicular** to the tangent, and every other point of the tangent lies outside the circle.
bullets: the tangent at $T$ is the **only** line through $T$ that does not enter the circle
from a point **inside** the circle no tangent can be drawn

visual.alt: A circle with centre O and radius 2.5 centimetres. A straight line touches the circle at T and is perpendicular to the radius OT. A point Q on the line, other than T, is joined to O by a dashed segment that is longer than the radius, so Q is outside the circle.
visual.caption: A tangent touches the circle at one point $T$ and is perpendicular to the radius $OT$; every other point of it is outside. Length in cm.

slides.narration: A tangent meets the circle in one point only, called the point of contact. The radius to that point is perpendicular to the tangent. Every other point of the tangent lies outside the circle, as the dashed line from O to Q shows, because it is longer than the radius. From a point inside a circle no tangent can be drawn at all.

slides.heading: Two tangents from an outside point
slides.body_md: From an outside point $P$ two tangents $PA$ and $PB$ can be drawn. They are **equal**, and the line $PO$ **bisects** the angle between them.
bullets: the right triangles $OAP$ and $OBP$ are congruent: same $OP$, same radius
so $\angle APO = \angle BPO$ and $\angle AOP = \angle BOP$

visual.alt: A circle with centre O and radius 2.5 centimetres, and an outside point P with OP equal to 6.5 centimetres. The tangents PA and PB are each 6 centimetres long, with one tick each, and meet the radii OA and OB at right angles.
visual.caption: From the external point $P$: $PA = PB = 6$ cm and $OA \perp PA$, $OB \perp PB$. Lengths in cm.

slides.narration: Here the circle has radius two point five centimetres and P is six point five centimetres from the centre. The tangents P A and P B are equal. The two right triangles share the side O P and have equal radii, so they are congruent. That gives equal tangents, and the line P O bisects the angle at P. Each tangent is six centimetres long, since six point five squared minus two point five squared is thirty six.

slides.heading: Steps of construction of the tangents
slides.body_md: The points of contact must see $OP$ at a **right angle**, so they lie on the circle with $OP$ as diameter.
bullets: join $OP$ and bisect it at $M$
draw the circle with centre $M$ and radius $MO$
it cuts the given circle at $A$ and $B$
join $PA$ and $PB$

nodes.label: Join OP
Bisect OP: perpendicular bisector, mid-point M
Circle with centre M through O and P
It cuts the given circle at A and B
Join PA and PB: the tangents

visual.alt: Flow chart of the construction of tangents from an external point: join O and P, bisect OP at M, draw the circle with centre M through O and P, mark where it cuts the given circle at A and B, and join P to A and to B.
visual.caption: Steps of construction of the tangents from $P$.

slides.narration: Here are the steps of construction. Join O to P and bisect it, with arcs of equal radius from O and from P, to get the mid point M. With centre M and radius M O draw a circle. It passes through O and P and cuts the given circle at two points, A and B. Join P to A and P to B. These are the two tangents.

slides.heading: The construction on the page
slides.body_md: Keep **every arc**: the marks are for the construction. The circle on $OP$ as diameter passes through $O$, $A$, $P$ and $B$.

visual.alt: Construction of the tangents from P to the circle with centre O and radius 3 centimetres, with OP equal to 5 centimetres. M is the mid-point of OP. The circle with centre M and radius 2.5 centimetres, drawn on OP as diameter, cuts the given circle at A and B. Joining PA and PB gives the two tangents.
visual.caption: Steps: bisect $OP$ at $M$; draw the circle with diameter $OP$; it cuts the circle at $A$ and $B$; join $PA$ and $PB$.

slides.narration: This is the finished construction for a circle of radius three centimetres and a point five centimetres from the centre. The mid point M of O P is two point five centimetres from each end. The circle about M cuts the given circle at A above and B below. The two tangents P A and P B are then drawn with a ruler. Leave all the arcs visible.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: measure and check
slides.body_md: Construct the tangents from $P$, $OP = 5$ cm, to a circle of radius $3$ cm. Measure $PA$ and $\angle APB$, and check by calculation.
bullets: **Step 1 —** $\angle OAP = 90^\circ$, so $PA = \sqrt{5^2 - 3^2} = \sqrt{16} = 4$ cm; measuring gives $PA = PB = 4.0$ cm.
**Step 2 —** $\sin\angle APO = \dfrac{3}{5} = 0.6$, so $\angle APO \approx 36.87^\circ$.
**Step 3 —** $\angle APB = 2 \times 36.87^\circ = 73.74^\circ$, which measures $74^\circ$ to the nearest degree.

visual.alt: A circle with centre O and radius 3 centimetres. P is a point outside the circle with OP equal to 5 centimetres. Two tangents PA and PB touch the circle at A and B; each is 4 centimetres long and carries one tick. The radii OA and OB are dashed and meet the tangents at right angles.
visual.caption: Two tangents from $P$ to a circle of radius $3$ cm: $PA = PB = 4$ cm. Lengths in cm.

slides.narration: In the right triangle O A P the longest side is five and one leg is three, so P A is the square root of sixteen, which is four centimetres. Measuring on the drawing gives the same. The sine of the angle at P is three over five, which is point six, so the angle is about thirty six point eight seven degrees. Doubling gives seventy three point seven four, so the angle between the tangents is seventy four degrees to the nearest degree.

slides.heading: Quick check: which circle?
slides.body_md: Which circle locates the points of contact?
slides.narration: Think about which circle passes through every point that sees the segment O P at a right angle.

slides.heading: Why the construction works
slides.body_md: Every point of the circle on $OP$ as diameter sees $OP$ at a **right angle** (angle in a semicircle). So at the point $A$ where it meets the given circle, $\angle OAP = 90^\circ$ and $PA$ is perpendicular to the radius $OA$: $PA$ is a tangent.

visual.alt: A circle with diameter OP of length 5 centimetres and centre M; A is a point on it and also on the given circle of radius 3 centimetres. The angle OAP is drawn as a right angle, because it is an angle in a semicircle. MA, MO and MP are each 2.5 centimetres.
visual.caption: Why it works: $A$ is on the circle with diameter $OP$, so $\angle OAP = 90^\circ$ (angle in a semicircle) and $PA$ touches the circle at $A$. Lengths in cm.

slides.narration: Here the circle with diameter O P has centre M and radius two point five centimetres. The point A is on this circle, so the angle O A P is an angle in a semicircle and is a right angle. A is also on the given circle, so O A is a radius. A line at a right angle to a radius at its end touches the circle, so P A is a tangent.

slides.heading: Quick check: tangent and radius
slides.body_md: What angle does the radius make with the tangent?
slides.narration: Recall the key property that links a tangent to the radius at its point of contact.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: tangents at a given angle
slides.body_md: Two tangents to a circle of radius $3$ cm are inclined at $60^\circ$. Find $OP$ and the length of each tangent.
bullets: **Step 1 —** $PO$ bisects the angle, so $\angle APO = 30^\circ$ and $\sin 30^\circ = \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{3}{OP}$.
**Step 2 —** $OP = 3 \div \dfrac{1}{2} = 6$ cm.
**Step 3 —** $PA = \sqrt{6^2 - 3^2} = \sqrt{27} \approx 5.2$ cm.

visual.alt: A circle with centre O and radius 3 centimetres. P is 6 centimetres from O. The two tangents PA and PB from P include an angle of 60 degrees at P. The radii OA and OB are dashed and meet the tangents at right angles.
visual.caption: Tangents inclined at $60^\circ$ to a circle of radius $3$ cm: $OP = 6$ cm. Lengths in cm.

slides.narration: The line P O bisects the sixty degree angle, so the angle at P in the right triangle is thirty degrees. The sine of thirty degrees is one half, which equals three over O P. So O P is three divided by one half, which is six centimetres. Then each tangent is the square root of six squared minus three squared, which is the square root of twenty seven, about five point two centimetres.

slides.heading: Quick check: equal tangents
slides.body_md: Which statement is true for every pair of tangents?
slides.narration: Compare the two right triangles formed with the centre.

slides.heading: Concentric circles and a touching chord
slides.body_md: Two circles with the **same centre** and radii $R > r$. A chord $PQ$ of the larger circle that touches the smaller circle at $T$ is **bisected** at $T$, because $OT \perp PQ$.

visual.alt: Two concentric circles with centre O, of radii 5 and 3 centimetres. A chord PQ of the larger circle touches the smaller circle at T. The radius OT of 3 centimetres is perpendicular to PQ, OP is 5 centimetres, and the chord PQ is 8 centimetres long.
visual.caption: A chord of the larger circle that touches the smaller one: $OT \perp PQ$, so $T$ bisects $PQ$ and $PQ = 8$. Lengths in cm.

slides.narration: Two circles share the centre O, with radii five and three centimetres. A chord P Q of the larger circle touches the smaller one at T. The radius O T is perpendicular to the chord, and a perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects it. So the chord is twice the square root of R squared minus r squared.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: a plank across a ring
slides.body_md: A plank is a chord of a circle of radius $5$ m and just touches a concentric circle of radius $3$ m. Find its length.
bullets: **Step 1 —** $OT \perp PQ$, so $PT = \sqrt{5^2 - 3^2} = \sqrt{16} = 4$ m.
**Step 2 —** $T$ is the mid-point, so $PQ = 2 \times 4 = 8$ m.

visual.alt: Two concentric circles with centre O, of radii 5 and 3 centimetres. A chord PQ of the larger circle touches the smaller circle at T. The radius OT of 3 centimetres is perpendicular to PQ, OP is 5 centimetres, and the chord PQ is 8 centimetres long.
visual.caption: A chord of the larger circle that touches the smaller one: $OT \perp PQ$, so $T$ bisects $PQ$ and $PQ = 8$. Lengths in cm.

slides.narration: The radius to the touching point is three metres and is perpendicular to the plank. In the right triangle O T P the longest side is five, so P T is the square root of twenty five minus nine, which is four metres. The touching point is the mid point of the plank, so the plank is two times four, which is eight metres long.

slides.heading: Quick check: a point inside
slides.body_md: How many tangents from a point inside the circle?
slides.narration: Compare the distance of the point from the centre with the radius.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: The radius to the point of contact is **perpendicular** to the tangent
Two tangents from $P$ are **equal** and $PO$ bisects the angle between them
Construction: circle on **$OP$ as diameter** cuts the circle at $A$ and $B$
Length $\sqrt{OP^2 - r^2}$; angle $\angle APB = 2\sin^{-1}\dfrac{r}{OP}$

rows: the radius to the point of contact is perpendicular to the tangent
circle on $OP$ as diameter cuts the circle at $A$ and $B$
a chord of the larger circle touching the smaller one is bisected at the point of contact

visual.alt: Summary table of part one: the radius to the point of contact is perpendicular to the tangent, giving the tangent length from the right triangle; the two tangents from an outside point are equal and the line to the centre bisects the angle between them; the circle on the line from the centre to the point as diameter cuts the circle at the points of contact; for concentric circles a chord of the larger circle touching the smaller is bisected at the point of contact and has length twice the square root of the difference of the squares of the radii.
visual.caption: Tangents: the facts and the construction on one card.

slides.narration: To sum up part one. The radius to the point of contact is perpendicular to the tangent. Two tangents from a point are equal and the line to the centre bisects the angle between them. To construct them draw the circle on O P as diameter, and join P to the two points where it cuts the circle. The tangent length comes from Pythagoras, and the angle from the sine ratio.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **Given figure (1–2 marks):** circle with the exact radius, $P$ at the exact distance
**Construction (2–3 marks):** perpendicular bisector of $OP$, the circle on $OP$, tangents joined; arcs left visible
**Measurement (1–2 marks):** tangent length to $0.1$ cm, angle to the nearest degree
**Mistake:** a bisecting radius smaller than half of $OP$, so the arcs do not cross
**Mistake:** drawing the second circle with centre $P$ instead of $M$
**Habit:** check $PA$ with $\sqrt{OP^2 - r^2}$
slides.narration: In the exam, draw the circle and the point with exact measurements. For the construction show the perpendicular bisector of O P, the circle on O P as diameter and the two tangents, with all arcs visible. Measure the tangent to a tenth of a centimetre. Common slips are using a radius smaller than half of O P so the arcs do not cross, and drawing the second circle about P instead of about the mid point.

decks.title: Constructions — Part 2: Circumcircle, incircle and the regular hexagon
goals: Construct the circumcircle of a triangle and say where its centre lies for acute, right and obtuse triangles
Construct the incircle of a triangle and measure its radius
Construct a regular hexagon and draw its circumcircle and incircle
Calculate and check the radii against the measured values

slides.heading: Circles of a triangle and a hexagon
slides.body_md: Every triangle has a circle **through its three corners**, the **circumcircle**, and a circle **touching its three sides**, the **incircle**. A regular hexagon has both too.

visual.alt: An equilateral triangle ABC of side 6 centimetres. The perpendicular bisectors of the sides meet at the centre O, which is also where the angle bisectors meet. The circumcircle passes through A, B and C.
visual.caption: Equilateral triangle: the perpendicular bisectors meet at the centre $O$. Lengths in cm.

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. Here is an equilateral triangle with side six centimetres. The perpendicular bisectors of its sides meet at the centre O, and the circle about O through the corners is the circumcircle. In this part we construct the circumcircle and the incircle of a triangle, and of a regular hexagon, and we measure their radii.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Construct the **circumcircle** with perpendicular bisectors
Construct the **incircle** with angle bisectors
Say where the **circumcentre** lies for each kind of triangle
Construct a **regular hexagon** with its two circles
slides.narration: These are your goals for part two. You will construct the circumcircle with perpendicular bisectors and the incircle with angle bisectors. You will say where the circumcentre lies for each kind of triangle. Finally you will construct a regular hexagon with its circumcircle and its incircle.

slides.heading: The circumcircle
slides.body_md: The perpendicular bisectors of the three sides meet at one point, the **circumcentre** $O$. It is equally far from the three corners, so the circle with centre $O$ and radius $OA$ passes through $A$, $B$ and $C$.

visual.alt: Triangle ABC with BC 6.5, CA 7 and AB 7.5 centimetres. The perpendicular bisectors of the sides meet at the circumcentre O inside the triangle. D, E and F are the mid-points of the sides. OA, OB and OC are dashed and carry one tick each because they are equal; the circle through A, B and C has centre O.
visual.caption: Circumcircle: the perpendicular bisectors of the sides meet at $O$, and $OA = OB = OC$. Lengths in cm.

slides.narration: The perpendicular bisector of a side holds every point equally far from the two ends of that side. The three bisectors meet at one point, O. So O is equally far from A, B and C, and the circle with centre O and radius O A passes through all three corners. The dashed segments carry one tick because they are equal. This circle is the circumcircle.

slides.heading: Steps of construction: circumcircle
slides.body_md: Two perpendicular bisectors are enough to fix $O$; the third is a check.

nodes.label: Draw the triangle to the given measurements
Perpendicular bisectors of two sides
They meet at the circumcentre O
Circle with centre O and radius OA
Measure the radius with a ruler

visual.alt: Flow chart for the circumcircle: draw the triangle, draw the perpendicular bisectors of two sides, they meet at the circumcentre O, draw the circle with centre O and radius OA, and measure the radius.
visual.caption: Steps of construction of the circumcircle.

slides.narration: First draw the triangle to the measurements given. Then draw the perpendicular bisectors of two of the sides, using equal arcs from each end. They meet at the circumcentre O. With centre O and radius O A draw the circle, which should pass through B and C as well. Finally measure the radius with a ruler.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: circumcircle of a triangle
slides.body_md: Construct triangle $ABC$ with $BC = 7$ cm, $AB = 5$ cm and $\angle B = 60^\circ$. Draw its circumcircle and measure the radius.
bullets: **Step 1 —** draw $BC$, make $\angle B = 60^\circ$ and cut $BA = 5$ cm; then $AC^2 = 7^2 + 5^2 - 2 \times 7 \times 5 \times \dfrac{1}{2} = 39$, so $AC \approx 6.2$ cm.
**Step 2 —** draw the perpendicular bisectors of $AB$ and $BC$; they meet at $O$ inside the triangle.
**Step 3 —** the circle with centre $O$ through $A$ passes through $B$ and $C$; its radius measures $3.6$ cm.

visual.alt: Triangle ABC with BC 7 centimetres, AB 5 centimetres and angle B equal to 60 degrees. The perpendicular bisectors of the sides meet at O inside the triangle and the circle with centre O passes through A, B and C.
visual.caption: Triangle with $BC = 7$, $AB = 5$, $\angle B = 60^\circ$ and its circumcircle. Lengths in cm.

slides.narration: Draw B C seven centimetres, make a sixty degree angle at B and cut B A five centimetres. By the cosine rule A C squared is thirty nine, so A C is about six point two centimetres. Draw the perpendicular bisectors of A B and B C. They meet at O inside the triangle. The circle about O through A also passes through B and C, and its radius measures about three point six centimetres.

slides.heading: Quick check: finding the circumcentre
slides.body_md: Which lines meet at the circumcentre?
slides.narration: Remember which lines are made of points equally far from two corners.

slides.heading: Where is the circumcentre?
slides.body_md: The position depends on the **largest angle**. If $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$ the triangle is right-angled; if $a^2 + b^2 < c^2$ it is obtuse.
bullets: **acute** triangle: $O$ is **inside**
**right** triangle: $O$ is the **mid-point of the hypotenuse**
**obtuse** triangle: $O$ is **outside**, beyond the longest side

visual.alt: An obtuse triangle ABC with BC 8, CA 5 and AB 4 centimetres, obtuse at A. The perpendicular bisectors of the sides meet at the circumcentre O, which lies outside the triangle, on the opposite side of BC from A. The circle through A, B and C has centre O.
visual.caption: Obtuse triangle: the circumcentre $O$ lies outside the triangle. Lengths in cm.

slides.narration: Here is a triangle with sides eight, five and four. Four squared plus five squared is forty one, which is less than eight squared, sixty four, so the triangle is obtuse. Its perpendicular bisectors meet outside the triangle, beyond the longest side. For an acute triangle the circumcentre is inside, and for a right triangle it is the mid point of the hypotenuse.

slides.heading: A right triangle: the hypotenuse is a diameter
slides.body_md: In a right triangle the circumcentre is the **mid-point of the hypotenuse**, so the hypotenuse is a **diameter** and $R = \dfrac{\text{hypotenuse}}{2}$.

visual.alt: A right-angled triangle ABC with the right angle at A, BC 10, CA 8 and AB 6 centimetres. The circumcentre O is the mid-point of the hypotenuse BC, so the circumcircle has BC as a diameter and radius 5 centimetres.
visual.caption: Right triangle: the circumcentre is the mid-point of the hypotenuse, $R = \dfrac{10}{2} = 5$. Lengths in cm.

slides.narration: This triangle has sides six, eight and ten. The right angle is at A. The circumcentre sits at the mid point of the hypotenuse B C, so the hypotenuse is a diameter of the circumcircle. The radius is half of ten, which is five centimetres. This is the converse of the angle in a semicircle.

slides.heading: The incircle
slides.body_md: The bisectors of the three angles meet at one point, the **incentre** $I$, which is equally far from the three **sides**. The circle with centre $I$ touching the sides is the **incircle**.

visual.alt: Triangle ABC with BC 6.5, CA 7 and AB 7.5 centimetres. The dashed bisectors of angles B and C meet at the incentre I. The two halves of angle B carry one arc each and the two halves of angle C carry two arcs each, showing that each angle is cut into two equal parts.
visual.caption: The bisectors of $\angle B$ and $\angle C$ meet at $I$; each angle is cut into two equal parts. Lengths in cm.

slides.narration: A point on an angle bisector is equally far from the two sides of the angle. The bisectors of the three angles meet at one point, the incentre I, which is equally far from all three sides. The circle about I that touches the sides is the incircle. In this figure the two halves of angle B carry one arc each, and the halves of angle C carry two arcs each.

slides.heading: Steps of construction: incircle
slides.body_md: Two angle bisectors fix $I$. The radius is the **perpendicular** distance from $I$ to a side.

nodes.label: Draw the triangle to the given measurements
Bisect two of the angles
Bisectors meet at the incentre I
Perpendicular from I to a side: foot D
Circle with centre I and radius ID

visual.alt: Flow chart for the incircle: draw the triangle, bisect two angles, the bisectors meet at the incentre I, draw the perpendicular from I to a side with foot D, and draw the circle with centre I and radius ID.
visual.caption: Steps of construction of the incircle.

slides.narration: Draw the triangle first. Bisect two of its angles with arcs and a ruler. The bisectors meet at the incentre I. From I draw a perpendicular to one side, which meets it at D. With centre I and radius I D draw the circle. It touches all three sides, each at the foot of a perpendicular from I.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: incircle and touching points
slides.body_md: Triangle $ABC$ has $BC = 6.5$ cm, $CA = 7$ cm and $AB = 7.5$ cm. Find the inradius and the lengths from each vertex to the points of contact.
bullets: **Step 1 —** $s = \dfrac{6.5 + 7 + 7.5}{2} = 10.5$ and the area is $\sqrt{10.5 \times 4 \times 3.5 \times 3} = \sqrt{441} = 21$ cm$^2$.
**Step 2 —** $r = \dfrac{21}{10.5} = 2$ cm; the drawing shows $ID = IE = IF = 2.0$ cm.
**Step 3 —** tangents from a vertex are equal: $AF = AE = s - a = 4$, $BD = BF = s - b = 3.5$, $CD = CE = s - c = 3$ (cm), and $4 + 3.5 = 7.5 = AB$.

visual.alt: Triangle ABC with BC 6.5, CA 7 and AB 7.5 centimetres. The dashed bisectors of the three angles meet at the incentre I, inside the triangle. The circle with centre I touches the sides at D on BC, E on CA and F on AB; each radius ID, IE, IF is 2 centimetres and is perpendicular to its side.
visual.caption: Incircle: the angle bisectors meet at $I$; $ID = IE = IF = 2$ cm and each radius is perpendicular to its side. Lengths in cm.

slides.narration: The semi perimeter is ten point five. The area by Heron is the square root of ten point five times four times three point five times three, which is twenty one. So the inradius is twenty one over ten point five, which is two centimetres. The two tangents from a vertex to the incircle are equal. From A they are ten point five minus six point five, which is four. From B they are three point five, and from C they are three.

slides.heading: Quick check: the incentre
slides.body_md: Where must the centre of the tank be?
slides.narration: The tank must be equally far from all three edges of the lawn.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: an equilateral triangle
slides.body_md: Construct an equilateral triangle of side $6$ cm. Draw its incircle and circumcircle and compare the radii.
bullets: **Step 1 —** the bisectors and the perpendicular bisectors are the same lines, so the circles have the **same centre**.
**Step 2 —** measuring gives $R \approx 3.5$ cm and $r \approx 1.7$ cm.
**Step 3 —** $R = 2r$: the circumcentre divides each height in the ratio $2 : 1$.

visual.alt: An equilateral triangle ABC of side 6 centimetres with its incircle. The centre I is where the angle bisectors meet, and the circle touches each side at its mid-point D, E or F.
visual.caption: Equilateral triangle: the incircle touches each side at its mid-point. Lengths in cm.

slides.narration: In an equilateral triangle each perpendicular bisector is also an angle bisector, so the circumcentre and the incentre are the same point. Measuring the radii on an accurate drawing gives about three point five centimetres for the circumcircle and about one point seven centimetres for the incircle. The circumradius is exactly twice the inradius.

slides.heading: The regular hexagon
slides.body_md: A regular hexagon is made of **six equilateral triangles** meeting at the centre $O$. So its side equals the radius of the circle through its corners, and each side subtends $60^\circ$ at $O$.

visual.alt: A regular hexagon ABCDEF of side 4 centimetres with centre O. The segments joining O to the six vertices are each 4 centimetres and cut the hexagon into six equilateral triangles; each angle at O is 60 degrees.
visual.caption: A regular hexagon is six equilateral triangles: $OA = OB = \dots = 4$ and each angle at $O$ is $60^\circ$. Lengths in cm.

slides.narration: A regular hexagon splits into six equilateral triangles that meet at the centre. Each triangle has all sides four centimetres here, and each angle at O is sixty degrees. So the distance from the centre to a corner equals the side. This is why a hexagon can be constructed by stepping the radius round a circle.

slides.heading: Steps of construction: regular hexagon
slides.body_md: The circle you draw is already the **circumcircle**.

sections.heading: 1. Tangent and radius
sections.body_md:
- A **tangent** meets a circle in **one** point, the **point of contact** $T$.
- The radius $OT$ is **perpendicular** to the tangent; every other point of the tangent is outside the circle.
- From a point on the circle there is **one** tangent; from a point inside there is **none**; from a point outside there are **two**.

*Example:* $OP = 5$, $r = 3$: $PT = \sqrt{5^2 - 3^2} = 4$.

key_terms.definition_md: A line that touches a circle at exactly one point.
The point where a tangent touches the circle; the radius to it is perpendicular to the tangent.

sections.heading: 2. Constructing tangents from an external point
sections.body_md:
- **Steps of construction:** join $OP$; bisect it at $M$; with centre $M$ and radius $MO$ draw a circle; it cuts the given circle at $A$ and $B$; join $PA$ and $PB$.
- **Why it works:** $A$ is on the circle with diameter $OP$, so $\angle OAP = 90^\circ$ (angle in a semicircle).
- The tangents are equal, $PA = PB$, and $PO$ bisects $\angle APB$.
- $\sin\angle APO = \dfrac{r}{OP}$, so $\angle APB = 2\sin^{-1}\dfrac{r}{OP}$ and $\angle AOB = 180^\circ - \angle APB$.

*Example:* $r = 3$, $OP = 5$: $PA = 4$, $\angle APB \approx 74^\circ$, $\angle AOB \approx 106^\circ$.

sections.heading: 3. Concentric circles
sections.body_md:
- A chord of the larger circle (radius $R$) that touches the smaller one (radius $r$) is **bisected** at the point of contact.
- Its length is $2\sqrt{R^2 - r^2}$.
- Tangents from a point of the **outer** circle to the **inner** circle are parts of such chords.

*Example:* $R = 5$, $r = 3$: chord $= 2 \times 4 = 8$.

sections.heading: 4. The circumcircle of a triangle
sections.body_md:
- The **perpendicular bisectors** of the sides meet at the **circumcentre** $O$; $OA = OB = OC = R$.
- **Steps:** draw the triangle; perpendicular bisectors of two sides meet at $O$; circle with centre $O$ and radius $OA$; measure $R$.
- Acute triangle: $O$ **inside**. Right triangle: $O$ is the **mid-point of the hypotenuse**, $R = \dfrac{c}{2}$. Obtuse triangle: $O$ **outside**.
- Check: $R = \dfrac{abc}{4 \times \text{area}}$.

*Example:* $BC = 7$, $AB = 5$, $\angle B = 60^\circ$: $R \approx 3.6$ cm.

sections.heading: 5. The incircle of a triangle
sections.body_md:
- The **angle bisectors** meet at the **incentre** $I$, equally far from the three sides; $ID = IE = IF = r$, each perpendicular to its side.
- **Steps:** draw the triangle; bisect two angles; they meet at $I$; draw $ID$ perpendicular to a side; circle with centre $I$ and radius $ID$.
- $r = \dfrac{\text{area}}{s}$ where $s$ is the semi-perimeter; for a right triangle $r = \dfrac{a + b - c}{2}$.
- Tangents from a vertex are equal: $AF = AE = s - a$.

*Example:* sides $6.5$, $7$, $7.5$: $s = 10.5$, area $21$, $r = 2$ cm.

sections.heading: 6. The regular hexagon
sections.body_md:
- A regular hexagon is **six equilateral triangles** around the centre $O$: side $a$, $R = a$, each angle at $O$ is $60^\circ$.
- **Steps:** circle of radius $a$ about $O$; mark $A$; with the same radius cut $B$, $C$, $D$, $E$, $F$ round the circle; join in order.
- The circle drawn is the **circumcircle**. The **incircle** has centre $O$ and radius $OM$ with $M$ the mid-point of a side: $r = a\sin 60^\circ = \dfrac{a\sqrt{3}}{2}$.
- Perimeter $6a$.

*Example:* $a = 4$: $R = 4$, $r = \sqrt{12} \approx 3.5$.

- Measure lengths to **0.1 cm** and angles to the **nearest degree**; write the unit.

- Keep every construction arc; label every point.
- Ring between two circles: $\pi(R^2 - r^2)$.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How marks are awarded**
- *Given figure (1–3 marks):* exact radius, lengths and angles.
- *Construction (2–4 marks):* perpendicular bisector of $OP$ and the circle on $OP$; or two perpendicular bisectors or two angle bisectors; arcs left visible.
- *Measurement and check (1–3 marks):* lengths to $0.1$ cm, angles to the nearest degree, with a calculation.
- *10-mark structured question:* parts (a), (b), (c), usually $3 + 3 + 4$: the figure, then the construction, then the measurements.

**Common mistakes**
1. Drawing the second circle with centre $P$ instead of the mid-point $M$ of $OP$.
2. Using angle bisectors for the circumcircle, or perpendicular bisectors for the incircle.
3. Measuring the inradius to a vertex instead of to a side.
4. Forgetting that the circumcentre of an obtuse triangle is outside it.
5. Taking the inradius of a hexagon as its side.
6. Rubbing out the construction arcs.

questions.stem_md: To draw the tangents from an external point $P$ to a circle with centre $O$, a second circle is drawn to locate the points of contact. Which circle is it?

options.text_md: the circle with $OP$ as a diameter
the circle with centre $O$ and radius $OP$
a circle with the mid-point of $OP$ as centre and the same radius as the given circle
the circle with centre $P$ and radius $OP$

questions.solution_md: The points of contact $A$ and $B$ must satisfy $\angle OAP = 90^\circ$, and every point that sees $OP$ at a right angle lies on the circle with $OP$ as diameter. So that circle, cut with the given circle, gives $A$ and $B$. The other three circles do not pass through $O$ and $P$ both, or have the wrong radius.

questions.stem_md: A straight rod $PA$ just touches a circular plate with centre $O$ at the point $A$. What is the size of the angle $OAP$ between the rod and the radius $OA$?
questions.solution_md: A tangent is perpendicular to the radius drawn to the point of contact, so $\angle OAP = 90^\circ$. The rod and the radius are not straight on one line (that would be $180^\circ$), and the other values have no reason to occur.

questions.stem_md: A circular pond (imagined) has radius $5$ m. A gardener stands $13$ m from its centre and walks along a straight path that just touches the pond. How far does the gardener walk from the starting point to the point where the path touches the pond?
questions.solution_md: The path is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact, so the centre, the gardener and the point of contact form a right triangle with hypotenuse $13$: $\sqrt{13^2 - 5^2} = \sqrt{144} = 12$ m. The value $8$ is $13 - 5$, $13.9$ is $\sqrt{13^2 + 5^2}$ rounded and $18$ is $13 + 5$.

questions.stem_md: $PA$ and $PB$ are the two tangents drawn from an outside point $P$ to a circle with centre $O$, touching it at $A$ and $B$. Which statement is true for every such pair of tangents?
questions.solution_md: The right triangles $OAP$ and $OBP$ share the hypotenuse $OP$ and have $OA = OB$, so $PA = PB$ always. The tangents are at right angles only in the special case $OP = r\sqrt{2}$, $PA$ is shorter than $OP$, and $\angle AOB + \angle APB = 180^\circ$, so those two angles are equal only when both are $90^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: While drawing the circle that passes through all three corners of a triangle, the centre of the circle is found as the meeting point of which three lines?

options.text_md: the perpendicular bisectors of the sides

questions.solution_md: A point on the perpendicular bisector of a side is equally far from the two ends of that side. The meeting point of the three perpendicular bisectors is therefore equally far from all three corners, so it is the centre of the circle through them. The angle bisectors give the incircle, and medians and altitudes give no circle centre.

questions.stem_md: A circular tank is to be sunk inside a triangular lawn so that it touches all three edges. Where must the centre of the tank be placed?

options.text_md: at the corner with the largest angle
where the three angle bisectors of the lawn meet
where the three perpendicular bisectors of the edges meet
at the mid-point of the longest edge

questions.solution_md: A point on an angle bisector is equally far from the two edges that form the angle. The meeting point of the three angle bisectors is equally far from all three edges, so a circle about it with that distance as radius touches all three. The perpendicular bisectors give the circle through the corners instead.

questions.stem_md: A triangular plot (imagined) has a right angle between boundary walls of lengths $8$ m and $15$ m. A circular fence passes through all three corners of the plot. What is the radius of the fence?
questions.solution_md: The longest side is $\sqrt{8^2 + 15^2} = \sqrt{289} = 17$ m, and in a right triangle the circumcentre is the mid-point of this hypotenuse, so the radius is $\dfrac{17}{2} = 8.5$ m. The value $17$ is the diameter, $11.5$ is the mean of the two walls and $7.5$ is half the longer wall.

questions.stem_md: A disc is to be cut from a right-angled triangular sheet of sides $6$ cm, $8$ cm and $10$ cm so that it just touches all three sides. What is the greatest possible radius of the disc?
questions.solution_md: The disc is the incircle, with radius $\dfrac{\text{area}}{\text{semi-perimeter}} = \dfrac{24}{12} = 2$ cm (also $\dfrac{6 + 8 - 10}{2} = 2$). The value $2.4$ is half the altitude to the hypotenuse, $4$ is $6 + 8 - 10$ without halving, and $1$ is the area divided by the whole perimeter.

questions.stem_md: A regular hexagon has each side $6$ cm long. What is the radius of the circle that passes through its six corners?
questions.solution_md: The centre and two neighbouring corners form an equilateral triangle, so the distance from the centre to a corner equals the side: $6$ cm. The value $3$ is half the side, $12$ is the diameter and $5.2$ is the radius of the incircle, not the circumcircle.

questions.stem_md: The incircle of a regular hexagon touches each side of the hexagon. Where does the circle touch a side?

options.text_md: at the point one third of the way along the side
at the mid-point of the side
at no definite point, because the circle crosses the side
at one of the two ends of the side

questions.solution_md: The radius to a point of contact is perpendicular to the side, and in a regular hexagon the perpendicular from the centre to a side meets it at its mid-point, by symmetry. The ends of the sides are the corners, which lie on the larger circle through the corners, outside the incircle.

questions.stem_md: A hexagonal floor tile (imagined) is a regular hexagon of side $8$ cm. A circular mat is to touch all six sides from inside. To the nearest $0.1$ cm, what is the radius of the mat?
questions.solution_md: The radius of the incircle is the perpendicular from the centre to a side. In the equilateral triangle formed by the centre and one side it is the height, $8 \sin 60^\circ = 6.9$ cm. The value $8$ is the radius of the circle through the corners, $4$ is half the side, and $9.2$ is $\dfrac{8}{\sin 60^\circ}$, which divides instead of multiplying.

questions.stem_md: A taut wire from a point $P$ just touches a circular pillar of radius $7$ cm. The point $P$ is $25$ cm from the axis of the pillar. How long is the wire between $P$ and the pillar?
questions.solution_md: The wire is a tangent, so it is at right angles to the radius at the point of contact: $\sqrt{25^2 - 7^2} = \sqrt{576} = 24$ cm. The value $18$ is $25 - 7$, $26$ is $\sqrt{25^2 + 7^2}$ rounded, and $32$ is $25 + 7$.

questions.stem_md: Two straight paths just touch a circular lawn of radius $2.5$ m and meet at a lamp post $5$ m from the centre of the lawn. What angle do the two paths make with each other at the lamp post?
questions.solution_md: Each path is a tangent, so the right triangle formed by the centre, the lamp post and a point of contact has $\sin\angle P = \dfrac{2.5}{5} = \dfrac{1}{2}$, so each half-angle is $30^\circ$ and the angle between the paths is $60^\circ$. The value $30^\circ$ forgets to double, and $120^\circ$ is the angle at the centre between the two points of contact.

questions.stem_md: A ring-shaped track lies between two concentric circles of radii $13$ m and $5$ m. A straight plank is laid so that its ends touch the outer circle and its middle just touches the inner circle. How long is the plank?
questions.solution_md: The plank is a chord of the outer circle touching the inner circle, so the radius to the touching point bisects it at a right angle. Half the plank is $\sqrt{13^2 - 5^2} = \sqrt{144} = 12$ m, so the plank is $2 \times 12 = 24$ m. The value $12$ is only half, $16$ is $2(13 - 5)$ and $26$ is the diameter of the outer circle.

questions.stem_md: An obtuse-angled triangular sail has its largest angle at $A$. Where does the centre of the circle through $A$, $B$ and $C$ lie?

options.text_md: outside the triangle, on the opposite side of $BC$ from $A$

questions.solution_md: The perpendicular bisectors of the sides of an obtuse triangle meet outside it, beyond the longest side $BC$. The centre is inside for an acute triangle and at the mid-point of the longest side only for a right triangle, and it can never be a vertex because it is equidistant from all three.

questions.stem_md: A signboard in the shape of an equilateral triangle has sides of $9$ cm. A thin wire ring passes through its three corners. To the nearest $0.1$ cm, what is the radius of the ring?
questions.solution_md: The circumcentre of an equilateral triangle is its centre, and the circumradius is $\dfrac{9}{\sqrt{3}} = 5.2$ cm, which is two thirds of the height $7.8$ cm. The value $4.5$ is half the side, $2.6$ is the inradius (one third of the height), and $7.8$ is the full height.

questions.stem_md: A triangular garden has sides $6.5$ m, $7$ m and $7.5$ m. A circular pond just touches all three sides from inside. What is the radius of the pond?
questions.solution_md: The semi-perimeter is $s = \dfrac{6.5 + 7 + 7.5}{2} = 10.5$ and the area is $\sqrt{10.5 \times 4 \times 3.5 \times 3} = \sqrt{441} = 21$, so the inradius is $\dfrac{21}{10.5} = 2$ m. The value $1$ divides by the whole perimeter, $4$ is $\dfrac{2 \times 21}{10.5}$, and $3.2$ is the area divided by the side $6.5$.

questions.stem_md: To fix the centre of the incircle of triangle $PQR$ with ruler and compasses, what is the least number of angle bisectors that you must draw?
questions.solution_md: Two lines meet in one point, so two angle bisectors already fix the incentre. A single bisector gives only a line of possible centres. The third bisector passes through the same point and only serves as a check, and six has no meaning here.

questions.stem_md: A hexagonal bolt head (imagined) is a regular hexagon with perimeter $30$ mm. What is the radius of the circle through its six corners?
questions.solution_md: The six sides are equal, so one side is $\dfrac{30}{6} = 5$ mm, and the radius of the circle through the corners equals the side: $5$ mm. The value $2.5$ is half the side, $6$ is the number of sides, and $4.3$ is the inradius $5 \sin 60^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: How many tangents can be drawn to a circle of radius $6$ cm from a point that is $4$ cm from its centre?
questions.solution_md: A point $4$ cm from the centre of a circle of radius $6$ cm is inside the circle. Every line through an inside point cuts the circle in two points, so none of them touches it, and no tangent exists. Two tangents exist only for a point outside, and one only for a point on the circle.

questions.stem_md: A tangent meets a circle in just one point. What is this point called?
questions.solution_md: The single common point of a tangent and the circle is the point of contact, and the radius drawn to it is perpendicular to the tangent. The external point is where two tangents start, outside the circle, and the centre is the middle of the circle.

questions.stem_md: In triangle $ABC$ the bisectors of angles $A$ and $B$ meet at $I$. What does the bisector of angle $C$ do?

options.text_md: it is parallel to the bisector of angle $A$
it meets the other two bisectors in two different points

questions.solution_md: The three angle bisectors of a triangle are concurrent: they meet at the incentre $I$, which is equally far from all three sides. So the third bisector passes through the point where the first two meet. It is not parallel to another bisector, and it is perpendicular to $AB$ only for special triangles.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** When tangents are drawn from $P$ to a circle with centre $O$, the points of contact lie on the circle that has $OP$ as a diameter.

**Reason (R):** A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at its point of contact, and an angle in a semicircle is a right angle.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true. Since $\angle OAP = 90^\circ$ at each point of contact, $A$ and $B$ see $OP$ at a right angle, which happens exactly for points of the circle on $OP$ as diameter. So R explains A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The circumcentre of an obtuse-angled triangle lies inside the triangle.

**Reason (R):** The circumcentre is the point where the perpendicular bisectors of the three sides meet.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: R is true: that is how the circumcentre is found. A is false: in an obtuse triangle the three perpendicular bisectors meet outside the triangle, beyond the longest side. So A is false but R is true.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In an equilateral triangle, the circumcentre and the incentre are the same point.

**Reason (R):** All three angles of an equilateral triangle are $60^\circ$.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true. The reason is that the perpendicular bisector of each side also bisects the opposite angle, because the triangle is symmetric about it; the fact that each angle is $60^\circ$ does not by itself show that, so R is true but is not the explanation of A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The two tangents from an outside point to a circle make equal angles with the line joining that point to the centre.

**Reason (R):** The two tangents from an outside point to a circle are always perpendicular to each other.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: A is true: the right triangles $OAP$ and $OBP$ are congruent, so $\angle APO = \angle BPO$. R is false: the angle between the tangents is $2\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{r}{d}\right)$, which is $90^\circ$ only when $d = r\sqrt{2}$; for $r = 3$ and $d = 5$ it is about $74^\circ$.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A regular hexagon of side $6$ cm has an incircle of radius $6$ cm.

**Reason (R):** The circle through the six corners of a regular hexagon has a radius equal to its side.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: R is true: the radius of the circle through the corners equals the side, $6$ cm. A is false: the incircle is smaller, with radius $6 \sin 60^\circ = 5.2$ cm, because it touches the sides at their mid-points and not at the corners.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A tangent drawn from a point $13$ cm from the centre of a circle of radius $5$ cm is $12$ cm long.

**Reason (R):** The two tangents drawn from an outside point to a circle are equal in length.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but R does not explain the value $12$: that comes from the right triangle, $\sqrt{13^2 - 5^2} = 12$, which uses the tangent being perpendicular to the radius. Equal tangents are a different fact.

questions.stem_md: Two different tangents can be drawn to a circle from a point that lies on the circle itself.
questions.solution_md: False. Through a point of the circle there is exactly one tangent, the line perpendicular to the radius at that point. Two tangents exist only for a point outside the circle.

questions.stem_md: For a regular hexagon of side $4$ cm, the circle that touches its sides from inside has a radius smaller than $4$ cm.
questions.solution_md: True. The radius of the incircle is $4 \sin 60^\circ \approx 3.5$ cm, which is less than the radius $4$ cm of the circle through the corners.

questions.stem_md: The centre of the incircle of a triangle is the same distance from the three corners of the triangle.
questions.solution_md: False. The incentre is the same distance from the three sides (the inradius), not from the corners. The point equidistant from the corners is the circumcentre, and the two points are different unless the triangle is equilateral.

questions.stem_md: A stick from a point $5$ cm away from the centre of a circle of radius $4$ cm just touches the circle. The length of the stick between the point and the circle is $3$ cm.
questions.solution_md: True. The stick is a tangent, so $\sqrt{5^2 - 4^2} = \sqrt{9} = 3$ cm.

questions.stem_md: In a right-angled triangle, the centre of the circle through the three corners is the vertex at the right angle.
questions.solution_md: False. The centre of the circumcircle of a right triangle is the mid-point of the hypotenuse, so the hypotenuse is a diameter. The vertex at the right angle is on the circle, not at its centre.

questions.stem_md: The perpendicular bisectors of the three sides of any triangle all pass through one point.
questions.solution_md: True. The meeting point of two perpendicular bisectors is equally far from all three corners, so it lies on the third perpendicular bisector too. This point is the circumcentre.

questions.stem_md: In a regular hexagon, the length of one side is half the radius of the circle through its six corners.
questions.solution_md: False. The side equals that radius, because the centre and two neighbouring corners form an equilateral triangle. A side that is half the radius would be too short to close the hexagon.

questions.stem_md: A cable from a hook $P$, $17$ m from the centre of a circular water tank of radius $8$ m, just touches the tank. The length of cable from $P$ to the point where it touches the tank is ___ m.
questions.solution_md: The cable is a tangent, perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact, so its length is $\sqrt{17^2 - 8^2} = \sqrt{225} = 15$ m.

questions.stem_md: A triangular metal plate has sides $5$ cm, $12$ cm and $13$ cm. The radius of the circle through its three corners is ___ cm.
questions.solution_md: $5^2 + 12^2 = 169 = 13^2$, so the triangle is right-angled and its hypotenuse $13$ is a diameter of the circle through the corners. The radius is $\dfrac{13}{2} = 6.5$ cm.

questions.stem_md: In a regular hexagon with centre $O$, each side subtends an angle of ___ degrees at $O$.
questions.solution_md: The six sides share the full turn of $360^\circ$ equally, so each subtends $\dfrac{360}{6} = 60^\circ$ at the centre.

questions.stem_md: A set square is a right-angled triangle with sides $9$ cm, $12$ cm and $15$ cm. The largest circle that fits inside it has radius ___ cm.
questions.solution_md: The largest circle inside is the incircle, with radius $\dfrac{9 + 12 - 15}{2} = 3$ cm for a right triangle (equivalently the area $54$ divided by the semi-perimeter $18$ is $3$).

questions.stem_md: The circle that passes through all three vertices of a triangle is called the ___ of the triangle.
questions.solution_md: A circle through all three vertices is the circumcircle, and its centre, the circumcentre, is the meeting point of the perpendicular bisectors of the sides.

questions.stem_md: A rope is stretched from a peg $P$ so that it just touches a circular fountain of radius $9$ m. The peg is $15$ m from the centre of the fountain. Find the length of rope between the peg and the fountain, in m.
questions.solution_md: The rope is a tangent, so it is at right angles to the radius at the point of contact and $\sqrt{15^2 - 9^2} = \sqrt{144} = 12$ m.

questions.stem_md: A ring-shaped garden lies between two circles with the same centre, of radii $17$ m and $8$ m. Find the length of the longest straight path that stays inside the garden and is a chord of the outer circle touching the inner circle, in m.
questions.solution_md: The radius to the touching point bisects the path at a right angle, so half the path is $\sqrt{17^2 - 8^2} = \sqrt{225} = 15$ m, and the whole path is $2 \times 15 = 30$ m.

questions.stem_md: A triangular glass pane has sides $7$ cm, $24$ cm and $25$ cm. Find the radius of the circular frame that passes through its three corners, in cm.
questions.solution_md: $7^2 + 24^2 = 625 = 25^2$, so the pane is right-angled and the longest side is a diameter of the frame. The radius is $\dfrac{25}{2} = 12.5$ cm.

questions.stem_md: A triangular plot has sides $13$ m, $14$ m and $15$ m. The largest circular flower bed that fits in the plot touches all three sides. Find its radius, in m.
questions.solution_md: The semi-perimeter is $\dfrac{13 + 14 + 15}{2} = 21$ and the area is $\sqrt{21 \times 8 \times 7 \times 6} = \sqrt{7056} = 84$, so the radius is $\dfrac{84}{21} = 4$ m.

questions.stem_md: A table-top is a regular hexagon of side $6$ cm in a model. A circular coaster touches all six sides from inside. Find its radius to the nearest $0.1$ cm.
questions.solution_md: The radius of the incircle is the height of the equilateral triangle formed by the centre and one side: $6 \sin 60^\circ = 5.2$ cm.

questions.stem_md: Two tangents to a circle of radius $5$ cm are inclined to each other at $60^\circ$. Find the distance, in cm, from the point where they meet to the centre of the circle.
questions.solution_md: The line to the centre bisects the $60^\circ$ angle, so each half-angle is $30^\circ$ and $\sin 30^\circ = \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{5}{OP}$. Hence $OP = 5 \div \dfrac{1}{2} = 10$ cm.

questions.stem_md: From a point $P$ that is $7.5$ cm from the centre $O$ of a circle of radius $4.5$ cm, a tangent $PT$ is drawn. Find the length $PT$, and name the property that lets you use a right triangle.

answer.model_answer_md:
The tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact, so $\angle OTP = 90^\circ$.

In the right triangle $OTP$: $PT = \sqrt{7.5^2 - 4.5^2} = \sqrt{36} = 6$ cm.

questions.solution_md: Tangent perpendicular to radius; Pythagoras in the triangle OTP.

marking_scheme.step: tangent perpendicular to the radius stated

questions.stem_md: A triangle has sides $9$ cm, $12$ cm and $15$ cm. State, with a reason, where the centre of its circumcircle lies, and find the circumradius.

answer.model_answer_md:
$9^2 + 12^2 = 225 = 15^2$, so the triangle is right-angled and the circumcentre is the mid-point of the hypotenuse $15$ cm.

The circumradius is $\dfrac{15}{2} = 7.5$ cm.

questions.solution_md: Converse of Pythagoras; the hypotenuse of a right triangle is a diameter of the circumcircle.

marking_scheme.step: right angle shown; circumcentre at the mid-point of the hypotenuse

questions.stem_md: A regular hexagon with side $7$ cm is drawn with its circumcircle and incircle. Find the radius of each circle, to $0.1$ cm.

answer.model_answer_md:
The radius of the circumcircle equals the side, $7$ cm, since the centre and two neighbouring corners form an equilateral triangle.

The incircle radius is the height of that triangle: $7 \sin 60^\circ \approx 6.1$ cm.

questions.solution_md: Circumradius equals the side; the inradius is side times sine of 60 degrees.

questions.stem_md: For an equilateral triangle of side $6$ cm, say where the centres of the circumcircle and the incircle lie in relation to each other, and compare the two radii.

answer.model_answer_md:
The perpendicular bisector of each side is also the bisector of the opposite angle, so the two centres coincide at the centre of the triangle.

Here the circumradius is $\dfrac{6}{\sqrt{3}} \approx 3.5$ cm and the inradius is $\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{3}} \approx 1.7$ cm, so the circumradius is twice the inradius, $R = 2r$.

questions.solution_md: Centres coincide; radii in the ratio 2 : 1.

questions.stem_md: A guy rope from the point $P$ is $10$ cm from the centre $O$ of a round post model of radius $6$ cm. The two taut strings from $P$ touch the post at $A$ and $B$. Find the length $PA$ and the angle $APB$ to the nearest degree.

answer.model_answer_md:
$PA = \sqrt{10^2 - 6^2} = \sqrt{64} = 8$ cm, since $\angle OAP = 90^\circ$.

In the right triangle $OAP$, $\sin\angle APO = \dfrac{6}{10} = 0.6$, so $\angle APO \approx 36.87^\circ$.

By symmetry $\angle APB = 2 \times 36.87^\circ = 73.74^\circ$, which is $74^\circ$ to the nearest degree.

questions.solution_md: Tangent length by Pythagoras; the half-angle at P from the sine ratio; double it.

questions.stem_md: From a point $P$ that is $13$ cm from the centre $O$ of a circle of radius $5$ cm, the tangents $PA$ and $PB$ are drawn. Find $PA$ and the area of the quadrilateral $OAPB$.

answer.model_answer_md:
$PA = \sqrt{13^2 - 5^2} = \sqrt{144} = 12$ cm.

The quadrilateral is two congruent right triangles $OAP$ and $OBP$, each with legs $5$ cm and $12$ cm.

Area $= 2 \times \dfrac{1}{2} \times 5 \times 12 = 60$ cm$^2$.

questions.solution_md: Two congruent right triangles share OP; add their areas.

questions.stem_md: A triangular steel plate has sides $5$ cm, $12$ cm and $13$ cm. Find the radius of the circle that passes through its corners and the radius of the largest circle that fits inside it.

answer.model_answer_md:
$5^2 + 12^2 = 169 = 13^2$, so the plate is right-angled; its circumradius is half the hypotenuse, $\dfrac{13}{2} = 6.5$ cm.

Area $= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 5 \times 12 = 30$ cm$^2$ and semi-perimeter $s = \dfrac{5 + 12 + 13}{2} = 15$ cm.

The inradius is $\dfrac{30}{15} = 2$ cm.

questions.solution_md: Circumradius is half the hypotenuse; inradius is area over semi-perimeter.

questions.stem_md: In triangle $ABC$, $BC = 8$ cm, $CA = 5$ cm and $AB = 4$ cm. Show that the centre of the circle through $A$, $B$ and $C$ lies outside the triangle, and measure the radius of that circle to $0.1$ cm.

answer.model_answer_md:
$AB^2 + CA^2 = 4^2 + 5^2 = 41$ and $BC^2 = 8^2 = 64$, and $41 < 64$, so $\angle A$ is obtuse.

The perpendicular bisectors of the sides of an obtuse triangle meet outside it, beyond the longest side $BC$, so the circumcentre is outside.

Drawing the perpendicular bisectors and the circle, the radius measures $4.9$ cm.

questions.solution_md: Compare the squares of the sides; the circumcentre of an obtuse triangle is outside; measure the radius.

questions.stem_md: A regular hexagon is constructed in a circle of radius $4.5$ cm by stepping the radius round the circumference. Find the side and the perimeter of the hexagon, and the radius of its incircle to $0.1$ cm.

answer.model_answer_md:
Each chord equals the radius, so the side is $4.5$ cm.

The perimeter is $6 \times 4.5 = 27$ cm.

The incircle radius is $4.5 \sin 60^\circ \approx 3.9$ cm.

questions.solution_md: Side equals the radius; perimeter is six sides; inradius from the equilateral triangle height.

questions.stem_md: $P$ is a point $6.5$ cm from the centre $O$ of a circle of radius $2.5$ cm. Describe how to construct the tangents from $P$, then find the length of a tangent and the angle between the two tangents, to the nearest degree.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Steps:** join $OP$ and bisect it at $M$; with centre $M$ and radius $MO$ draw a circle; it cuts the given circle at $A$ and $B$; join $PA$ and $PB$.

$PA = \sqrt{6.5^2 - 2.5^2} = \sqrt{36} = 6$ cm, since $\angle OAP = 90^\circ$ (angle in the semicircle on $OP$).

$\sin\angle APO = \dfrac{2.5}{6.5} = \dfrac{5}{13}$, so $\angle APO \approx 22.62^\circ$ and $\angle APB = 2 \times 22.62^\circ = 45.24^\circ \approx 45^\circ$.

questions.solution_md: Circle on OP as diameter; Pythagoras for the length; sine ratio for the half-angle.

marking_scheme.step: OP bisected at M; circle on OP as diameter

questions.stem_md: Two circles have the same centre $O$, with radii $10$ cm and $6$ cm. A chord $PQ$ of the larger circle touches the smaller one at $T$. Find $PQ$ and the angle $POQ$ at the centre, to the nearest degree.

answer.model_answer_md:
$OT \perp PQ$ and $OT = 6$ cm, so $T$ is the mid-point of $PQ$ and $PT = \sqrt{10^2 - 6^2} = \sqrt{64} = 8$ cm.

Hence $PQ = 2 \times 8 = 16$ cm.

In the right triangle $OTP$, $\cos\angle POT = \dfrac{6}{10} = 0.6$, so $\angle POT \approx 53.13^\circ$.

$\angle POQ = 2 \times 53.13^\circ = 106.26^\circ \approx 106^\circ$.

questions.solution_md: The radius to the touching point bisects the chord at a right angle; Pythagoras, then the cosine of the half-angle.

marking_scheme.step: T is the mid-point of PQ; PT = 8 cm

questions.stem_md: Triangle $ABC$ has $BC = 6.5$ cm, $CA = 7$ cm and $AB = 7.5$ cm. After constructing its circumcircle (centre $O$) and its incircle (centre $I$), state both radii to $0.1$ cm, and the distance $OI$ that you measure.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Steps:** draw the perpendicular bisectors of two sides to find $O$ and the circle through $A$, $B$, $C$; draw the bisectors of two angles to find $I$ and the circle touching the sides.

The area is $21$ cm$^2$ and $s = 10.5$ cm, so the inradius is $\dfrac{21}{10.5} = 2$ cm, which the drawing shows as $2.0$ cm.

The circumradius is $\dfrac{6.5 \times 7 \times 7.5}{4 \times 21} = 4.0625$ cm, so it measures $4.1$ cm.

The two centres are close but different, and $OI$ measures $0.5$ cm.

questions.solution_md: Perpendicular bisectors for the circumcentre, angle bisectors for the incentre; check both radii with area formulas.

questions.stem_md: Construct triangle $ABC$ with $BC = 7$ cm, $\angle B = 60^\circ$ and $AB = 5$ cm. Draw its circumcircle and incircle, and write down the two radii to the nearest $0.1$ cm.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Triangle:** draw $BC = 7$ cm, make $\angle CBX = 60^\circ$ and cut $BA = 5$ cm on $BX$; join $AC$. Then $AC^2 = 7^2 + 5^2 - 2 \times 7 \times 5 \times \dfrac{1}{2} = 39$, so $AC \approx 6.2$ cm.

**Circumcircle:** the perpendicular bisectors of $AB$ and $BC$ meet at $O$ inside the triangle; the circle with centre $O$ through $A$ passes through $B$ and $C$, and its radius measures $3.6$ cm.

**Incircle:** the bisectors of $\angle B$ and $\angle C$ meet at $I$; the perpendicular from $I$ to $BC$ gives the radius, $1.7$ cm.

questions.solution_md: SAS triangle; perpendicular bisectors give the circumcircle and angle bisectors the incircle; the cosine rule checks AC.

questions.stem_md: A regular hexagon of side $5$ cm is drawn with its circumcircle and incircle. Find the radius of each circle, and the area of the ring between the two circles, taking $\pi = 3.14$ and giving the area to $0.1$ cm$^2$.

answer.model_answer_md:
The radius of the circumcircle equals the side: $R = 5$ cm.

The incircle radius $r$ satisfies $r^2 = 5^2 - 2.5^2 = 18.75$ (right triangle with hypotenuse $5$ and a leg of half a side), so $r \approx 4.3$ cm.

The ring has area $\pi(R^2 - r^2) = 3.14 \times (25 - 18.75) = 19.625 \approx 19.6$ cm$^2$.

questions.solution_md: Inradius squared from Pythagoras, then the ring area as the difference of the two disc areas.

questions.stem_md: In the right-angled triangle with sides $9$ cm, $12$ cm and $15$ cm, $O$ is the centre of the circle through the three corners and $I$ is the centre of the circle touching the three sides. Find both radii, and measure $OI$ to $0.1$ cm.

answer.model_answer_md:
Take the right-angle vertex $A$ as the origin with the legs along the axes, $B = (9, 0)$ and $C = (0, 12)$. The circumcentre is the mid-point of $BC$, so $O = (4.5, 6)$ and $R = \dfrac{15}{2} = 7.5$ cm.

The inradius is $\dfrac{9 + 12 - 15}{2} = 3$ cm, so the incentre, $3$ cm from each leg, is $I = (3, 3)$.

Then $OI^2 = (4.5 - 3)^2 + (6 - 3)^2 = 1.5^2 + 3^2 = 11.25$, so $OI \approx 3.4$ cm.

questions.solution_md: Coordinates with the right angle at the origin: circumcentre at the mid-point of the hypotenuse, incentre at (r, r).

questions.stem_md: A flagpole $P$ stands $25$ cm from the centre $O$ of a circular disc of radius $7$ cm in a model, and two strings from $P$ touch the disc at $A$ and $B$. Find the length of one string, the angle between the strings and the angle $AOB$, each angle to the nearest degree.

answer.model_answer_md:
$PA = \sqrt{25^2 - 7^2} = \sqrt{576} = 24$ cm.

$\sin\angle APO = \dfrac{7}{25} = 0.28$, so $\angle APO \approx 16.26^\circ$ and $\angle APB = 2 \times 16.26^\circ = 32.52^\circ \approx 33^\circ$.

In the quadrilateral $OAPB$ the angles at $A$ and $B$ are right angles, so $\angle AOB = 180^\circ - 32.52^\circ = 147.48^\circ \approx 147^\circ$.

questions.solution_md: Tangent length by Pythagoras; the sine ratio for the half-angle; the angle sum of the kite for the angle at the centre.

questions.stem_md:
Use a ruler and a pair of compasses.

(a) Draw a circle with centre $O$ and radius $4.5$ cm, and mark a point $P$ with $OP = 7.5$ cm.

(b) Construct the two tangents from $P$ to the circle, leaving all arcs visible, and name the points of contact $A$ and $B$.

(c) Measure $PA$, $PB$ and $\angle APB$, and check the length $PA$ by calculation.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** With the compass point at $O$ and radius $4.5$ cm draw the circle. Mark $P$ so that $OP = 7.5$ cm and join $OP$.

**(b)** *Steps of construction:* draw the perpendicular bisector of $OP$ (arcs of equal radius greater than $3.75$ cm from $O$ and from $P$); it meets $OP$ at $M$, where $OM = 3.75$ cm. With centre $M$ and radius $MO$ draw a circle. It cuts the given circle at $A$ and $B$. Join $PA$ and $PB$: these are the tangents.

**(c)** Measuring gives $PA = PB = 6.0$ cm and $\angle APB \approx 74^\circ$. Check: $\angle OAP = 90^\circ$, so $PA = \sqrt{7.5^2 - 4.5^2} = \sqrt{36} = 6$ cm. Also $\sin\angle APO = \dfrac{4.5}{7.5} = 0.6$, so $\angle APO \approx 36.87^\circ$ and $\angle APB = 73.74^\circ \approx 74^\circ$.

questions.solution_md: Circle on OP as diameter locates the points of contact; Pythagoras and the sine ratio check the measurements.

Use a ruler and a pair of compasses.

(a) Draw a circle with centre $O$ and radius $3.5$ cm and mark a point $P$ at a distance of $7$ cm from $O$.

(b) Construct the tangents $PA$ and $PB$ from $P$ to the circle.

(c) Measure $PA$ and $\angle APB$, and calculate the area of the quadrilateral $OAPB$ to $0.1$ cm$^2$.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Draw the circle of radius $3.5$ cm about $O$ and mark $P$ with $OP = 7$ cm.

**(b)** *Steps:* bisect $OP$ at $M$; with centre $M$ and radius $MO = 3.5$ cm draw a circle (it passes through $O$ and $P$); it cuts the given circle at $A$ and $B$; join $PA$ and $PB$.

**(c)** Measuring gives $PA = 6.1$ cm and $\angle APB = 60^\circ$. Check: $\angle OAP = 90^\circ$, so $PA^2 = 7^2 - 3.5^2 = 36.75$ and $PA \approx 6.1$ cm; and $\sin\angle APO = \dfrac{3.5}{7} = \dfrac{1}{2}$, so $\angle APO = 30^\circ$ and $\angle APB = 60^\circ$. The area of $OAPB$ is $2 \times \dfrac{1}{2} \times 3.5 \times 6.06 \approx 21.2$ cm$^2$.

questions.stem_md:
Use a ruler and a pair of compasses.

(a) Draw two concentric circles with centre $O$ and radii $6.5$ cm and $2.5$ cm. Mark a point $P$ on the outer circle.

(b) Construct the two tangents from $P$ to the inner circle, touching it at $A$ and $B$, and extend them to meet the outer circle again at $Q$ and $R$.

(c) Measure $PA$, $PQ$ and $\angle OPA$ (to the nearest degree), and show by calculation why $A$ is the mid-point of $PQ$.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Draw both circles about $O$ and mark $P$ on the outer circle, so $OP = 6.5$ cm.

**(b)** *Steps:* join $OP$ and bisect it at $M$; with centre $M$ and radius $MO = 3.25$ cm draw a circle; it cuts the inner circle at $A$ and $B$; join and extend $PA$ and $PB$ to meet the outer circle at $Q$ and $R$.

**(c)** Measuring gives $PA = 6.0$ cm, $PQ = 12.0$ cm and $\angle OPA \approx 23^\circ$. Calculation: $\angle OAP = 90^\circ$, so $PA = \sqrt{6.5^2 - 2.5^2} = \sqrt{36} = 6$ cm and $\sin\angle OPA = \dfrac{2.5}{6.5} = \dfrac{5}{13}$, so $\angle OPA \approx 22.62^\circ$. Since $OA \perp PQ$ and $PQ$ is a chord of the outer circle, the perpendicular from the centre bisects it: $AQ = \sqrt{6.5^2 - 2.5^2} = 6 = PA$, so $PQ = 12$ cm.

questions.solution_md: Tangent from a point of the outer circle to the inner circle; the perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord PQ.

Use a ruler and a pair of compasses.

(a) Construct triangle $ABC$ with $AB = 7$ cm, $BC = 6$ cm and $CA = 5$ cm.

(b) Draw the circumcircle of the triangle, showing the perpendicular bisectors, and measure its radius to $0.1$ cm.

(c) Draw the incircle, showing the angle bisectors, and measure its radius to $0.1$ cm. Measure the distance between the two centres.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Draw $AB = 7$ cm. With centre $A$ and radius $5$ cm and with centre $B$ and radius $6$ cm draw arcs meeting at $C$; join $AC$ and $BC$.

**(b)** Draw the perpendicular bisectors of $AB$ and $BC$ (equal arcs from each end); they meet at $O$. With centre $O$ and radius $OA$ draw the circle through $A$, $B$ and $C$. Measuring gives $R = 3.6$ cm.

**(c)** Bisect $\angle A$ and $\angle B$; the bisectors meet at $I$. Drop a perpendicular from $I$ to a side and draw the circle touching all three sides. The radius measures $r = 1.6$ cm, and $OI \approx 1.0$ cm, so the centres are different points. Check: $s = 9$, area $= \sqrt{9 \times 2 \times 3 \times 4} = \sqrt{216}$, so $r = \dfrac{\sqrt{216}}{9} \approx 1.63$ cm.

questions.solution_md: SSS triangle; perpendicular bisectors for the circumcircle; angle bisectors for the incircle; Heron checks the radius.

questions.stem_md:
Use a ruler, a set square and a pair of compasses.

(a) Construct triangle $ABC$ with $AB = 6$ cm, $BC = 8$ cm and $\angle ABC = 90^\circ$, and measure $AC$.

(b) Draw the circumcircle. Where is its centre, and what is its radius?

(c) Draw the incircle and measure its radius. Taking $B$ as the origin with $BC$ along the $x$-axis, find the distance between the centres of the two circles.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Draw $BC = 8$ cm, erect the perpendicular at $B$ and cut $BA = 6$ cm; join $AC$. Measuring gives $AC = \sqrt{6^2 + 8^2} = \sqrt{100} = 10$ cm.

**(b)** Bisect $AB$ and $BC$ perpendicularly; the bisectors meet at $O$, which is the mid-point of the hypotenuse $AC$. The circle through $A$, $B$ and $C$ has $AC$ as diameter, so $R = \dfrac{10}{2} = 5$ cm.

**(c)** Bisect $\angle A$ and $\angle C$ to find $I$ and draw the circle touching the sides: its radius measures $2.0$ cm, which agrees with $r = \dfrac{6 + 8 - 10}{2} = 2$ cm. With $B = (0, 0)$, $C = (8, 0)$, $A = (0, 6)$ we get $O = (4, 3)$ and $I = (2, 2)$, so $OI^2 = (4 - 2)^2 + (3 - 2)^2 = 5$ and $OI = \sqrt{5} \approx 2.2$ cm.

questions.solution_md: Right angle at B; the circumcentre is the mid-point of the hypotenuse; the incentre is r from both legs; coordinates give OI.

questions.stem_md:
Use a ruler, a protractor and a pair of compasses.

(a) Construct triangle $ABC$ with $BC = 6$ cm, $AB = 4$ cm and $\angle ABC = 120^\circ$, and measure $AC$ to $0.1$ cm.

(b) Draw the circumcircle. State whether its centre $O$ lies inside or outside the triangle, and measure the radius to $0.1$ cm.

(c) Draw the incircle and measure its radius to $0.1$ cm.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Draw $BC = 6$ cm, make $\angle CBX = 120^\circ$ and cut $BA = 4$ cm on $BX$; join $AC$. By the cosine rule $AC^2 = 6^2 + 4^2 - 2 \times 6 \times 4 \times \cos 120^\circ = 52 + 24 = 76$, so $AC \approx 8.7$ cm.

**(b)** Draw the perpendicular bisectors of $AB$ and $BC$; they meet at $O$, which is **outside** the triangle on the far side of $AC$ from $B$ (because $\angle B$ is obtuse), at a distance of $2.5$ cm from $AC$. The circle with centre $O$ through $A$ has radius $R \approx 5.0$ cm.

**(c)** The bisectors of $\angle A$ and $\angle B$ meet at $I$ inside the triangle. The perpendicular from $I$ to a side gives the radius of the incircle, $r \approx 1.1$ cm. Check: area $= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 6 \times 4 \times \sin 120^\circ \approx 10.39$ and $s \approx 9.36$, so $r = \dfrac{10.39}{9.36} \approx 1.1$ cm.

questions.stem_md:
Use a ruler and a pair of compasses.

(a) Construct a regular hexagon $ABCDEF$ of side $6$ cm.

(b) Draw its circumcircle and its incircle.

(c) Measure the radius of the incircle to $0.1$ cm, and find the area of the ring between the two circles, taking $\pi = 3.14$ and giving the answer to $0.1$ cm$^2$.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** *Steps of construction:* with centre $O$ and radius $6$ cm draw a circle. Mark $A$ on it. With the same radius and centre $A$ cut the circle at $B$; with centre $B$ cut it at $C$; continue to $D$, $E$ and $F$. Join $AB$, $BC$, $CD$, $DE$, $EF$ and $FA$: each chord equals the radius, $6$ cm.

**(b)** The circle drawn in (a), through all six vertices, is the circumcircle, with radius $R = 6$ cm. Bisect $AB$ perpendicularly at $M$ and join $OM$; with centre $O$ and radius $OM$ draw the incircle, which touches every side at its mid-point.

**(c)** $OM$ measures $5.2$ cm. Check: $OM^2 = 6^2 - 3^2 = 27$ and $OM \approx 5.20$ cm. The ring area is $\pi(R^2 - r^2) = 3.14 \times (36 - 27) = 3.14 \times 9 = 28.26 \approx 28.3$ cm$^2$.

questions.solution_md: Chords equal to the radius step round the circle; the inradius squared is 36 minus 9; the ring is the difference of the two circles.
